summary: Astros is a website that acts like an educational resource, and a survival guide for astronauts. Among all the things you can find on Mars, Astros includes information about: Craters, climate, atmosphere, temperature, orbit, radiation, natural & artificial satellites & rovers. It also comes with a survival guide that shows spots where you can: find ice & water, use them as shelters against radiation, build a human base in the future, or simply avoid them due to containing seismic risk.

UAM – AMERICAN UNIVERSITY 

                         

NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026. 

Challenge´s name

Interplanetary Survival Guide: Martian Map

Team´s name

Los space-ialitos 

Members

  • Kristel Mayerlin Ubau Lopez
  • Stalin Josué Córdoba Guillén
  • Keyner Josué Velásquez
  • Nicolás Rafael Laguna Vallejos
  • Hady Nahomi Cruz Aguirre 

Date: November 15th 2026

Managua, Nicaragua. 

1. Proposal Summary

             Future human explorations of Mars will require tools that facilitate understanding the environment, identifying resources, and assessing potential risks. Although NASA has a large amount of scientific information available, it is distributed across different platforms, making it difficult for the general public to interpret.

             ASTROS is an interactive web platform that allows users to explore Mars and the Solar System through three-dimensional visualizations. It integrates geographical, environmental, and scientific information, along with tools for identifying natural resources, potential shelters, settlement areas, and risks present on the Martian surface.

            The platform also incorporates a rover route planner, information about space missions, orbital simulations, and an educational assistant called Astrocat.

Its purpose is to facilitate learning and bring users closer to the challenges of exploring and surviving on Mars.

2. Problem and Objectives

2.1. Context and Problem

  • - Exploring Mars requires understanding factors such as terrain, environmental conditions, water availability, and radiation exposure. Although scientific tools such as NASA Mars Trek exist, specialized information can be complex for users without technical knowledge.
  • - ASTROS aims to bring these elements together in an interactive experience, making it easier to understand Martian conditions and the challenges involved in establishing a human presence on the planet.

2.2. General Objective

  •  To develop an interactive web platform that integrates scientific information and three-dimensional visualizations to facilitate the exploration of Mars and the Solar System, promoting learning about the conditions and challenges of future space missions.

2.3. Specific Objectives 

  • Represent geographical features, landing sites, and space missions through interactive models.
  • Identify natural resources, potential shelters, and candidate areas for human settlements.
  • Incorporate route-planning tools that allow users to analyze distances, slopes, and terrain characteristics.
  • Facilitate understanding of astronomical phenomena through simulations and educational content.

3. Developed Solution 

ASTROS is an interactive web platform that allows users to explore Mars and the Solar System through three-dimensional visualizations and scientific information presented in an accessible way.

Its survival guide integrates layers showing water resources, potential shelters against radiation, candidate areas for human settlements, and seismic risks. It also incorporates conceptual infrastructure proposals and a rover route planner that estimates distances, slopes, and travel times.

The platform also allows users to consult information about space missions, satellites, and planets, as well as view orbital simulations and trips to Mars.

As an educational complement, it includes Astrocat, an interactive mascot that guides users through a tutorial and 50 questions with predetermined answers. All these features aim to facilitate understanding of the challenges of space exploration.

4. Methodology and Scientific Resources 

4.1. Alluvial Fan 

The National Aeronautics and Space Administration (n.d.) explains that:

Alluvial fans are well-defined landforms created by the deposition of loose material transported by water. They form broad, gently sloping ramps that extend from the outlets of mountainous drainage basins toward lower-lying basins.

When water reaches these basins, it usually arrives in the form of intense rainstorms or sudden floods caused by melting snow. This results in the rapid transportation of coarse material, which is deposited near the outlet due to the sharp decrease in stream energy as it leaves its confined channel, as well as the temporary nature of these floods.

The successive accumulation of layers and lobes of transported material eventually forms a fan. Alluvial fans originate in a subaerial environment, which distinguishes them from fan deltas, which form when a stream flows into a standing body of water.

They also differ from fans formed by debris flows. These originate from gravity-driven flows in which the material is supported by a matrix (generally clay-based), unlike water-dominated flows, which transport sediments both along the bed and in suspension.

4.2. Distribution of Aqueous Minerals 

According to the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (n.d.), "aqueous minerals are those that form in water, either through the chemical alteration of pre-existing rocks or through precipitation from a solution." The National Aeronautics and Space Administration also mentions that "the minerals that form depend on temperature, salinity, pH, and the composition of the parent rock. Therefore,  the aqueous minerals present on Mars provide important clues for understanding past environments."

This layer shows the distribution of silica (purple), phyllosilicates (blue), sulfates (orange), chloride (yellow), and carbonates (green). Spectrometric observations were collected from a variety of instruments, including CRISM aboard the Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter (National Aeronautics and Space Administration, n.d.). 

4.3. Dune Fields 

The National Aeronautics and Space Administration reports that:

The Mars Global Digital Dune Database provides a comprehensive and quantitative overview of the geographical distribution of medium- to large-sized dune fields, covering latitudes from 65° N to 65° S and including approximately 550 dune fields.

In future versions, the database will be expanded to cover the entire planet. Although an effort was made to include all dune fields located between 65° N and 65° S, some may have been excluded for two reasons.

Incomplete coverage of daytime infrared data from the THEMIS instrument may have resulted in the exclusion of certain medium- to large-sized dune fields. Additionally, the resolution of this coverage (100 m/pixel) inevitably led to the exclusion of smaller dune fields.

The smallest dune fields recorded in the database have an approximate area of 1 km². Although medium- to large-sized dune fields probably represent the largest accumulation of sediments on the planet, other smaller deposits may exist and could be identified using higher-resolution data.

Therefore, it should be noted that the database excludes all small dune fields, as well as some medium- to large-sized ones. Consequently, the absence of mapped dune fields does not mean that they do not exist, nor should it be interpreted as an absence of saltating sand in other areas.

4.4. Distribution of Gullies 

In the case of Mars, the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (n.d.) states the following: 

Gullies in the mid- and high-latitudes of Mars were first observed in 1997 in images captured by the Mars Orbiter Camera (MOC) aboard the Mars Global Surveyor (MGS) spacecraft.

Apparently geologically young (based on their overlapping relationships with wind-related formations and the absence of impact craters in most of them), these gullies quickly attracted the attention of the Martian scientific community because their formation could suggest the presence of liquid water.

This interpretation is based on the distinctive morphological characteristics of gullies, which include incised channels (many of them winding and with raised edges), as well as terraces and hydrodynamic features that indicate the passage of a fluid.

The possibility that liquid water existed on Mars in the geologically recent past (and perhaps even today, judging by the activity currently observed in these gullies) is significant because it has implications for the planet's past and present habitability.

Although the morphology of these channels was initially interpreted as evidence that liquid water played a role in their formation, the difficulty of maintaining water on the surface under recent Martian climatic conditions led to the proposal of several explanatory models, including "dry" mass-wasting processes and mechanisms related to carbon dioxide (CO₂).

4.5. Materials Containing Chloride Salts

In the case of Mars, the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (n.d.) states the following: 

The formation of chloride salts through evaporative precipitation in a basin may occur as a result of the accumulation of surface runoff or the emergence of groundwater.

On Mars, chloride salt deposits could also form through hydrothermal brines, where meteoric water interacts with heat from volcanism, impact events, or hot ash deposits (whether of volcanic origin or resulting from an impact).

The release of volatile elements from magma or lava flows, under reducing and high-temperature conditions, can generate surface crusts composed mainly of halide salts near fumaroles.

Finally, chloride salts can form through atmospheric interactions by efflorescence, similar to the thin layers and surface crusts (formed at a later stage) discovered by the Opportunity rover in Meridiani Planum.

This image shows the distribution of gullies on Mars based on more than 54,000 images from the Context Camera (CTX) aboard the Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter (MRO), covering approximately 85% of the Martian surface at a resolution of approximately 6 (National Aeronautics and Space Administration, n.d.).

5. Development, Results, and Evidence 

The ASTROS project: Atlas of Mars and the Solar System consists of developing an interactive web platform whose purpose is to facilitate the exploration and understanding of the planet Mars through the integration of scientific information, geographical resources, and visualization tools.

The proposal aims to provide users with a digital environment where they can learn about the planet's characteristics, identify natural resources, and explore possible locations for establishing future human bases.

For the development of the platform, information was organized into different sections that allow users to access content intuitively.

The main screen includes an information panel presenting general data about the environmental conditions on Mars, including temperature, precipitation, wind speed, radiation, atmospheric pressure, atmospheric composition, gravity, and the duration of a Martian day (sol).

Likewise, an exploration interface was implemented, allowing users to switch between the visualization of Mars and the Solar System, adjust the map's zoom level, and access different thematic sections.

These sections include the survival guide, geography, resources, date, satellites, and routes. The possibility of viewing the platform in both Spanish and English was also considered.

One of the main components of the project is the survival layers section, which presents different elements of interest for human exploration of Mars.

These layers include the identification of potential sources of ice and water, natural shelters against radiation, candidate locations for establishing human bases, and areas related to seismic activity.

Similarly, information about specific geographical regions of interest was incorporated, such as Arcadia, Deuteronilus, and Hebrus Valles, which are considered candidate locations for future bases.

Potential shelters against radiation are also presented in locations such as Arsia Mons, Pavonis Mons, and Hellas Planitia.

Finally, the platform includes conceptual proposals for infrastructure development on Mars, represented through designs of underground residential areas, industrial mining facilities, and energy zones.

These elements help illustrate possible alternatives for utilizing resources and establishing human settlements on the planet.

As a result of the project, a published web platform accessible through a browser was developed under the name ASTROS. It integrates information about Mars, geographical exploration tools, and content related to the planning of future missions and human settlements in a single environment.

Main Results Achieved 

  • Centralization of Scientific Information: A space is available that brings together different physical and environmental characteristics of Mars, making them easier to access and understand. 
  • Geographical Exploration: Visualization elements were incorporated to allow users to explore different regions of the planet and identify locations relevant to exploration. 
  • Identification of Resources and Areas of Interest: The proposal includes thematic layers related to water, ice, radiation, and potential locations for establishing human bases. 
  • Representation of Possible Settlements: Conceptual designs of residential, industrial, and energy infrastructure were included to illustrate alternatives for human development on Mars. 
  • Accessibility and Understanding: Organizing content into different sections and incorporating language options allows information to be presented in a more organized and accessible way. 

In general terms, the final product is an educational and informative digital tool that aims to bring users closer to understanding Mars and the challenges involved in its exploration and potential habitability.

In this way, ASTROS represents a proposal that combines scientific communication, geographical visualization, and conceptual planning for possible extraterrestrial settlements.

To support the development and results achieved, visual and documentary evidence of the final product is presented. This evidence demonstrates the platform's structure, the incorporated features, and the operation of its main tools. 


6. Impact and Future Outlook 

  1. Beneficiaries:  The platform is aimed at students, teachers, and the general public interested in space exploration. It can also serve as a conceptual reference for researchers and teams studying the planning of human missions. 
  2. Applications: Its main purpose is educational and simulation-based: it allows users to explore a real region of Mars, compare routes, and understand how terrain and environmental conditions influence a mission. 

It does not replace professional navigation or safety systems. 

  1. Future Outlook:  In the short term, the plan is to improve the map layers and incorporate information about dust storms.

In the medium term, the goal is to develop more accurate estimates of mobility, time, and resources.

In the long term, the experience will be expanded to other regions of Mars and to the Moon, incorporating new planning and training features.
